claim: The medial thalamus (MThal), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and striatum play important roles in affective-motivational pain processing and reward learning.
source: The medial thalamus (MThal), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and striatum play important roles in affective-motivational pain processing and reward learning.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established scientific understanding about these brain regions.

claim: Mu-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists potently inhibited MThal inputs without affecting ACC inputs to individual striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs).
source: Mu-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists potently inhibited MThal inputs without affecting ACC inputs to individual striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments as stated in the abstract.

claim: MOR activation inhibited MThal inputs to the pyramidal neurons in the ACC.
source: MOR activation also inhibited MThal inputs to the pyramidal neurons in the ACC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments as stated in the abstract.

claim: Delta-opioid receptor (DOR) agonists disinhibited ACC pyramidal neuron responses to MThal inputs by suppressing local feed-forward GABA signaling from parvalbumin-positive interneurons.
source: In contrast, delta-opioid receptor (DOR) agonists disinhibited ACC pyramidal neuron responses to MThal inputs by suppressing local feed-forward GABA signaling from parvalbumin-positive interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments as stated in the abstract.

claim: DOR activation in the ACC facilitated poly-synaptic (thalamo-cortico-striatal) excitation of MSNs by MThal inputs.
source: As a result, DOR activation in the ACC facilitated poly-synaptic (thalamo-cortico-striatal) excitation of MSNs by MThal inputs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments as stated in the abstract.

claim: Opioid effects on pain and reward may be shaped by the relative selectivity of opioid drugs to the specific circuit components.
source: These results suggest that opioid effects on pain and reward may be shaped by the relative selectivity of opioid drugs to the specific circuit components.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Opioids blunt both sensory-discriminative and affective-motivational dimensions of pain by modulating neuronal activity in the central and peripheral nervous systems.
source: Opioids blunt both sensory-discriminative and affective-motivational dimensions of pain by modulating neuronal activity in the central and peripheral nervous systems (Oertel et al., 2008; Zubieta et al., 2001; Corder et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The affective-motivational dimension of pain underlies the aversiveness and negative emotional affect that arise in response to activation of nociceptive inputs.
source: The affective-motivational dimension of pain underlies the aversiveness and negative emotional affect that arise in response to activation of nociceptive inputs (Gracely, 1992; Navratilova and Porreca, 2014; Treede et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In humans, affective pain perception is associated with increased activity in the medial thalamus and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
source: In humans, affective pain perception is associated with increased activity in the medial thalamus, as well as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) (Casey et al., 1994; Davis et al., 1997; Peyron et al., 1999; Peyron et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In rodents, chronic pain is associated with hypersensitivity of mediodorsal thalamic neurons to sensory stimuli.
source: In rodents, chronic pain is associated with hypersensitivity of mediodorsal thalamic neurons to sensory stimuli (Whitt et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Activation of the ACC has been shown to be aversive using a conditioned place aversion paradigm.
source: activation of the ACC has been shown to be aversive using a conditioned place aversion paradigm (Johansen and Fields, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Lesions of the ACC decrease affective-motivational pain responses.
source: In contrast, lesions of the ACC decrease affective-motivational pain responses (Johansen et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neurons from the medial thalamus (MThal) send glutamate afferents to the cortical regions, including the dorsal and ventral ACC, prefrontal cortex (PFC) and insular cortices.
source: Anatomically, neurons from the medial thalamus (MThal) send glutamate afferents to the cortical regions, including the dorsal and ventral ACC, prefrontal cortex (PFC) and insular cortices (Hunnicutt et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neurons from the medial thalamus send glutamate afferents to the dorsomedial striatum (DMS).
source: Anatomically, neurons from the medial thalamus (MThal) send glutamate afferents to the cortical regions, including the dorsal and ventral ACC, prefrontal cortex (PFC) and insular cortices (Hunnicutt et al., 2014), as well as to the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) (Hunnicutt et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The ACC projects to the DMS, forming a circuit connecting the MThal and the ACC, both of which provide convergent glutamate inputs to the DMS.
source: The ACC in turn projects to the DMS, forming a circuit connecting the MThal and the ACC, both of which provide convergent glutamate inputs to the DMS.
evidence: This statement is supported by the anatomical description and citations in the text.

claim: The thalamo-cortico-striatal circuit has been demonstrated to be involved in pain processing, in particular, affective pain perception.
source: This thalamo-cortico-striatal circuit has been demonstrated to be involved in pain processing, in particular, affective pain perception (Rainville et al., 1997; Price, 2000; Fields, 2004; Zhang et al., 2015; Yokota et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mu-opioid receptors (MORs) and delta-opioid receptors (DORs) are predominantly expressed in the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus and ACC, respectively.
source: Mu-opioid receptors (MORs) and delta-opioid receptors (DORs) are predominantly expressed in the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus and ACC, respectively (Mansour et al., 1994; Erbs et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Injection of opioids into the MD or ACC can relieve pain and induce conditioned place preference in an animal model of chronic pain.
source: Injection of opioids into the MD or ACC can relieve pain and induce conditioned place preference in an animal model of chronic pain (Carr and Bak, 1988; Guo et al., 2008; Navratilova et al., 2015a)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The striatum is enriched in MORs and DORs, as well as the endogenous opioid ligand enkephalin.
source: The striatum is enriched in MORs and DORs, as well as the endogenous opioid ligand enkephalin (Pert et al., 1976; Koshimizu et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Opioids have been shown to inhibit glutamate inputs to the striatum, as well as GABA release from local striatal circuitry.
source: Also, opioids have been shown to inhibit glutamate inputs to the striatum, as well as GABA release from local striatal circuitry (Jiang and North, 1992; Hoffman and Lupica, 2001; Brundege and Williams, 2002; Miura et al., 2007; Atwood et al., 2014; Banghart et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The striatum serves as a potentially critical hub for opioid-dependent modulation of fast synaptic transmission in the affective pain circuitry.
source: In this context, the striatum serves as a potentially critical hub for opioid-dependent modulation of fast synaptic transmission in the affective pain circuitry (Zubieta et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research and inference from the context.

claim: Application of [Met5]-enkephalin (ME, 3 µM) significantly decreased the amplitude of the EPSCs in striatal MSNs.
source: Similar to previously published results in the nucleus accumbens and dorsolateral striatum, application of the mu- and delta-selective opioid agonist [Met5]-enkephalin (ME, 3 µM) significantly decreased the amplitude of the EPSCs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments.

claim: The inhibition of EPSCs by ME was reversed upon washout of ME.
source: This inhibition was reversed upon washout of ME (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c; ME: 77.8 ± 4.6% of baseline; washout: 90.5 ± 2.6% of baseline; baseline vs ME: W(11) = 1, p<0.01) (Jiang and North, 1992; Hoffman and Lupica, 2001; Brundege and Williams, 2002).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support.

claim: The AMPA receptor antagonist NBQX (3 µM) eliminated the evoked currents.
source: The AMPA receptor antagonist NBQX (3 µM) eliminated the evoked currents (Figure 1—figure supplements 1c and 4.0 ± 2.6% of baseline; baseline vs NBQX: W(5) = 0, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support.

claim: Glutamate inputs from the medial thalamus and ACC converged in the DMS.
source: Anatomic mapping in mice indicated that glutamate inputs from the medial thalamus and ACC converged in the DMS (Figure 1a–b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–e) (Hunnicutt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's anatomical experiments, supported by figures and a citation.

claim: DAMGO inhibited oEPSC amplitude from MThal stimulation in a reversible manner.
source: The MOR-selective agonist DAMGO inhibited oEPSC amplitude to MThal stimulation (470 nm light) in a reversible manner, and did not alter oEPSC amplitude to ACC stimulation (Figure 1c; DAMGO IMThal: 38.2 ± 6.1% of baseline, z = 4.738, p<0.001; IACC: 92.8 ± 4.9%, z = 0.459, p=0.647).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: DAMGO did not alter oEPSC amplitude to ACC stimulation.
source: The MOR-selective agonist DAMGO inhibited oEPSC amplitude to MThal stimulation (470 nm light) in a reversible manner, and did not alter oEPSC amplitude to ACC stimulation (Figure 1c; DAMGO IMThal: 38.2 ± 6.1% of baseline, z = 4.738, p<0.001; IACC: 92.8 ± 4.9%, z = 0.459, p=0.647).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: DPDPE did not inhibit the ACC or MThal inputs to striatal MSNs.
source: Despite the apparent expression of DORs in the midline cortical regions, DOR activation by its selective agonist DPDPE did not inhibit the ACC, or MThal inputs (Figure 1b–d; DPDPE IMThal: 99.6 ± 5.7% of baseline, z = 0.106, p=0.916; IACC: 95.6 ± 2.6%, z = 0.196, p=0.845).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: DAMGO decreased oEPSC amplitude from the MThal inputs while it had no effect on oEPSCs from the PFC inputs.
source: DAMGO decreased oEPSC amplitude from the MThal inputs while it had no effect on oEPSCs from the PFC inputs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h–i; DAMGO IMThal: 22.2 ± 3.7% of baseline, z = 3.497, p<0.001; IPFC: 93.9 ± 5.6%, z = 0.052, p=0.958).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: DPDPE produced no significant changes in oEPSC amplitude from either MThal or PFC inputs to striatal MSNs.
source: DPDPE produced no significant changes in oEPSC amplitude from either input (DPDPE IMThal: 96.5 ± 3.9% of baseline, z = 0.087, p=0.931; IPFC: 81.6 ± 3.9%, z = 0.672, p=0.502).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support.

claim: MThal glutamate inputs onto MSNs were preferentially inhibited by activation of MORs.
source: These results indicate that MThal glutamate inputs onto MSNs were preferentially inhibited by activation of MORs, while DOR agonists had little to no modulatory effect on the MThal, ACC, or PFC inputs to the MSNs in the DMS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: DOR agonists had little to no modulatory effect on the MThal, ACC, or PFC inputs to the MSNs in the DMS.
source: These results indicate that MThal glutamate inputs onto MSNs were preferentially inhibited by activation of MORs, while DOR agonists had little to no modulatory effect on the MThal, ACC, or PFC inputs to the MSNs in the DMS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Activation of MORs by DAMGO, but not DORs by DPDPE, resulted in inhibition of the MThal inputs to the MSNs in Slc17a6-cre mice.
source: Similar to the results from wild-type mice, activation of MORs by DAMGO, but not DORs by DPDPE, resulted in inhibition of the MThal inputs to the MSNs (Figure 2; IDAMGO: 18.1 ± 3.9% of baseline, W(6) = 0, p<0.05; IDPDPE: 100.5 ± 7.9%, W(5) = 7, p=1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: MOR agonists inhibited inputs from the anterior medial thalamus to the DMS.
source: Furthermore, MOR agonists also inhibited inputs from the anterior medial thalamus, suggesting the general effects of opioid inhibition of thalamic inputs to the DMS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Single neuron tracing in the rat has demonstrated that medial thalamic neurons can send collaterals to both the cortex and striatum.
source: Single neuron tracing in the rat has demonstrated that medial thalamic neurons can send collaterals to both the cortex and striatum (Otake and Nakamura, 1998; Kuramoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Retrogradely labeled somas were found in the lateral MD and the central lateral (CL) thalamus following retrograde bead injections into the ACC and DMS.
source: Retrogradely labeled somas were found in the lateral MD and the central lateral (CL) thalamus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–g).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's anatomical experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: 21 ± 4% of striatal-projecting neurons colocalized with ACC-projecting neurons in the MD thalamus.
source: In brain sections containing the MD thalamus (selected figures 44, 45, and 46 of the Franklin and Paxinos atlas, second edition; Figure 3—figure supplement 1d), there was a substantial fraction of neurons that projected to the DMS that also contained retrograde beads originating from the ACC (21 ± 4% of striatal-projecting neurons colocalized with ACC-projecting neurons).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's anatomical experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: TdTomato-positive neurons were found in the MThal following injection of rAAV-retro-Cre in the ACC and AAV-FLEX-TdTomato in the MThal.
source: Indeed, TdTomato-positive neurons were found in the MThal (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's anatomical experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: TdTomato-expressing axon terminals, originating from thalamic neurons, were visible in the ACC.
source: GFP expression in the ACC indicated the rAAV-retro virus injection site (Figure 3c), and TdTomato-expressing axon terminals, originating from thalamic neurons, were also visible in the ACC (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's anatomical experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: GFP-expressing axons originating from the ACC and TdTomato-expressing axon collaterals originating from the MThal were observed in the DMS.
source: Prominent GFP-expressing axons originating from the ACC and TdTomato-expressing axon collaterals originating from the MThal were observed in the DMS (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's anatomical experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: There exist thalamic neurons that project to both the ACC and DMS.
source: These results indicate the existence of thalamic neurons that project to both the ACC and DMS, and further, that ACC-striatal and MThal-striatal projections can innervate anatomically overlapping areas in the DMS (Hunnicutt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical experiments and supported by a citation.

claim: ACC-striatal and MThal-striatal projections can innervate anatomically overlapping areas in the DMS.
source: These results indicate the existence of thalamic neurons that project to both the ACC and DMS, and further, that ACC-striatal and MThal-striatal projections can innervate anatomically overlapping areas in the DMS (Hunnicutt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical experiments and supported by a citation.

claim: Optical illumination evoked glutamate-mediated EPSCs in striatal MSNs that were potently inhibited by ME.
source: Optical illumination evoked glutamate-mediated EPSCs in striatal MSNs that were potently inhibited by ME (Figure 3f; IME: 22.4 ± 6.6% of baseline, N = 3, n = 5, paired t-test, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: There exists an opioid-sensitive thalamic neuronal population projecting to both the DMS and ACC.
source: These data suggest the existence of an opioid-sensitive thalamic neuronal population projecting to both the DMS and ACC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Inputs from the MD thalamus synapse directly onto layer 2/3 (L2/3) and 5 (L5) pyramidal neurons in the ACC.
source: Inputs from the MD thalamus have been reported to synapse directly onto layer 2/3 (L2/3) and 5 (L5) pyramidal neurons, and also to trigger GABA release onto pyramidal neurons via innervation of L2/3 and L5 parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons in the ACC (Delevich et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Inputs from the MD thalamus trigger GABA release onto pyramidal neurons via innervation of L2/3 and L5 parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons in the ACC.
source: Inputs from the MD thalamus have been reported to synapse directly onto layer 2/3 (L2/3) and 5 (L5) pyramidal neurons, and also to trigger GABA release onto pyramidal neurons via innervation of L2/3 and L5 parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons in the ACC (Delevich et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: oEPSCs of the L2/3 and L5 pyramidal neurons in the ACC from the MThal inputs were potently inhibited by the MOR agonist DAMGO.
source: Similar to the results from recordings of the MSNs in the DMS, oEPSCs of the L2/3 and L5 pyramidal neurons in the ACC from the MThal inputs were potently inhibited by the MOR agonist DAMGO but unaffected by the DOR agonist DPDPE, suggesting expression of MORs but not DORs on thalamic glutamate terminals in the ACC (Figure 4b–c, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–c; IDAMGO: 54.0 ± 5.0% of baseline, W(17) = 1, p<0.001; IDPDPE: 93.4 ± 7.0%, W(14) = 36, p=0.312; L2/3; IDAMGO: 69.3 ± 3.3% of baseline, W(15) = 0, p<0.001; IDPDPE: 92.9 ± 5.4%, W(9) = 9, p=0.129).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support and reference to figures.

claim: oEPSCs of the L2/3 and L5 pyramidal neurons in the ACC from the MThal inputs were unaffected by the DOR agonist DPDPE.
source: Similar to the results from recordings of the MSNs in the DMS, oEPSCs of the L2/3 and L5 pyramidal neurons in the ACC from the MThal inputs were potently inhibited by the MOR agonist DAMGO but unaffected by the DOR agonist DPDPE, suggesting expression of MORs but not DORs on thalamic glutamate terminals in the ACC (Figure 4b–c, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–c; IDAMGO: 54.0 ± 5.0% of baseline, W(17) = 1, p<0.001; IDPDPE: 93.4 ± 7.0%, W(14) = 36, p=0.312; L2/3; IDAMGO: 69.3 ± 3.3% of baseline, W(15) = 0, p<0.001; IDPDPE: 92.9 ± 5.4%, W(9) = 9, p=0.129).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support and reference to figures.

claim: MORs but not DORs are expressed on thalamic glutamate terminals in the ACC.
source: Similar to the results from recordings of the MSNs in the DMS, oEPSCs of the L2/3 and L5 pyramidal neurons in the ACC from the MThal inputs were potently inhibited by the MOR agonist DAMGO but unaffected by the DOR agonist DPDPE, suggesting expression of MORs but not DORs on thalamic glutamate terminals in the ACC (Figure 4b–c, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–c; IDAMGO: 54.0 ± 5.0% of baseline, W(17) = 1, p<0.001; IDPDPE: 93.4 ± 7.0%, W(14) = 36, p=0.312; L2/3; IDAMGO: 69.3 ± 3.3% of baseline, W(15) = 0, p<0.001; IDPDPE: 92.9 ± 5.4%, W(9) = 9, p=0.129).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Both DAMGO and DPDPE potently inhibited GABA-mediated oIPSCs from the MThal to the ACC pyramidal neurons.
source: Surprisingly, both DAMGO and DPDPE potently inhibited GABA-mediated oIPSCs from the MThal to the ACC pyramidal neurons (Figure 4e–f and Figure 4—figure supplement 1e–f; IDAMGO, 37.9 ± 7.8% of baseline, W(14) = 0, p< 0.001; IDPDPE, 47.6 ± 7.9%, W(11) = 1, p<0.01; IDAMGO, 61.2 ± 9.5% of baseline, W(12) = 1, p<0.001; IDPDPE, 62.7 ± 5.4%, W(10) = 0, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support and reference to figures.

claim: PV-positive neurons contribute to feed-forward inhibition of MThal inputs to L5 pyramidal neurons in the ACC.
source: Since PV-positive neurons reportedly contribute to feed-forward inhibition of MThal inputs to L5 pyramidal neurons in the ACC (Delevich et al., 2015), opioid modulation of oIPSCs of PV neurons onto L5 pyramidal neurons in the ACC was measured.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: oIPSCs from PV neurons to L5 pyramidal neurons in the ACC were potently inhibited by DPDPE but not DAMGO.
source: The oIPSCs were potently inhibited by DPDPE but not DAMGO (Figure 5b–c; IDAMGO: 104.1 ± 6.1% of baseline, W(11) = 25, p=0.998; IDPDPE: 44.9 ± 5.7%, W(15) = 0, p<0.001), suggesting that DORs were expressed on PV neurons in the ACC.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: DORs are expressed on PV neurons in the ACC.
source: The oIPSCs were potently inhibited by DPDPE but not DAMGO (Figure 5b–c; IDAMGO: 104.1 ± 6.1% of baseline, W(11) = 25, p=0.998; IDPDPE: 44.9 ± 5.7%, W(15) = 0, p<0.001), suggesting that DORs were expressed on PV neurons in the ACC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: 88.7 ± 1.4% of Pvalb-positive cells expressed detectable levels of Oprd1.
source: Images of fluorescent RNA probes for endogenous DORs (Oprd1) and parvalbumin (Pvalb) revealed that the majority of Pvalb-positive cells were also Oprd1-positive (Figure 5d,f; 88.7 ± 1.4% of Pvalb-positive cells expressed detectable levels of Oprd1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in situ hybridization experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: 95.0 ± 1.2% of parvalbumin protein-positive neurons expressed detectable levels of GFP in DOR-GFP knockin mice.
source: Similarly, 95.0 ± 1.2% of parvalbumin protein-positive neurons expressed detectable levels of GFP (Figure 5e–f).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's immunohistochemistry experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: DORs are expressed on PV neurons.
source: Together, these data indicate that DORs are expressed on PV neurons, consistent with their role in inhibition of GABA release onto pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry experiments.

claim: Activation of MORs by DAMGO decreased the fraction of trials that evoked action potentials in ACC L5 pyramidal neurons.
source: When APs were elicited in approximately 50% of the trials, activation of MORs by DAMGO decreased the fraction of trials that evoked action potentials (0.4 ± 0.1 fold change relative to baseline, paired t-test, p<0.01)
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support.

claim: Activation of DORs by DPDPE led to a significant increase in AP firing probability in ACC L5 pyramidal neurons.
source: while activation of DORs by DPDPE led to a significant increase in AP firing probability (5 ± 3.1 fold change relative to baseline, paired t-test, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support.

claim: MOR activation has an inhibitory effect on pyramidal neuron firing rates.
source: This was consistent with an inhibitory effect of MOR activation and a disinhibitory effect of DOR activation on pyramidal neuron firing rates (Figure 6b–c) with no significant effect on action potential latency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: DOR activation has a disinhibitory effect on pyramidal neuron firing rates.
source: This was consistent with an inhibitory effect of MOR activation and a disinhibitory effect of DOR activation on pyramidal neuron firing rates (Figure 6b–c) with no significant effect on action potential latency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: DOR activation in the ACC resulted in disinhibition of the pyramidal neurons within the ACC, which led to increased cortical excitability.
source: Thus, DOR activation in the ACC resulted in disinhibition of the pyramidal neurons within the ACC, which led to increased cortical excitability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Application of DPDPE increased the charge transfer of the poly-synaptic MThal→ACC→DMS oEPSCs.
source: Application of DPDPE increased the charge transfer of the poly-synaptic MThal→ACC→DMS oEPSCs (Figure 7b–c; Qbaseline: 129.4 ± −46.2 fC; QDPDPE: 344.7 ± 90.5 fC, W(7) = 2, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: MORs and DORs are present in the thalamo-cortico-striatal circuitry.
source: Taken together, the results indicate the presence of both MORs and DORs in the thalamo-cortico-striatal circuitry, where DORs primarily facilitated information flow in the indirect pathway from the MThal via the ACC to the DMS, while MORs suppressed information flow from the MThal directly to the DMS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: DORs primarily facilitated information flow in the indirect pathway from the MThal via the ACC to the DMS.
source: Taken together, the results indicate the presence of both MORs and DORs in the thalamo-cortico-striatal circuitry, where DORs primarily facilitated information flow in the indirect pathway from the MThal via the ACC to the DMS, while MORs suppressed information flow from the MThal directly to the DMS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: MORs suppressed information flow from the MThal directly to the DMS.
source: Taken together, the results indicate the presence of both MORs and DORs in the thalamo-cortico-striatal circuitry, where DORs primarily facilitated information flow in the indirect pathway from the MThal via the ACC to the DMS, while MORs suppressed information flow from the MThal directly to the DMS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: MOR and DOR activation are predicted to play opposing roles in pain processing mediated by the thalamo-cortico-striatal circuit.
source: Thus, MOR and DOR activation are predicted to play opposing roles in pain processing mediated by the thalamo-cortico-striatal circuit.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings.

claim: Projections from the MThal and ACC converged in the DMS, rather than the ventral striatum.
source: We found that projections from the MThal and ACC converged in the DMS, rather than the ventral striatum which has been well studied for reward and drug addiction.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's anatomical experiments.

claim: Activation of MORs suppressed both MThal-ACC and MThal-DMS excitatory synapses.
source: Specifically, activation of MORs suppressed both MThal-ACC and MThal-DMS excitatory synapses, however, activation of DORs enhanced the excitatory input from the MThal to the pyramidal neurons in the ACC by disinhibiting local feed-forward inhibition mediated by PV interneurons in the ACC.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Activation of DORs enhanced the excitatory input from the MThal to the pyramidal neurons in the ACC by disinhibiting local feed-forward inhibition mediated by PV interneurons in the ACC.
source: Specifically, activation of MORs suppressed both MThal-ACC and MThal-DMS excitatory synapses, however, activation of DORs enhanced the excitatory input from the MThal to the pyramidal neurons in the ACC by disinhibiting local feed-forward inhibition mediated by PV interneurons in the ACC.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: DOR-mediated disinhibition of MThal-ACC synapses facilitates information to flow from the MThal to the DMS via the ACC.
source: This DOR-mediated disinhibition of MThal-ACC synapses has functional significance at the network level in that it facilitates information to flow from the MThal to the DMS via the ACC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Single MSNs in the DMS can receive inputs from both the midline cortex and medial thalamus.
source: Here, we demonstrated that single MSNs in the DMS can receive inputs from both the midline cortex and medial thalamus.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments.

claim: In mice single thalamic neurons can project to both the cortex and striatum.
source: Consistent with studies demonstrating cortical and striatal projections for midline thalamic neurons in rats (Otake and Nakamura, 1998; Kuramoto et al., 2017), the simultaneous retrograde bead injections localized to the rostromedial ACC and DMS demonstrated double-labeling of individual neurons in the lateral MD and CL thalamus, suggesting that in mice single thalamic neurons can project to both the cortex and striatum.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's anatomical experiments supported by citations.
